name: Pedro Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Pedro. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a continuous miner at the Felton potash mine, 900 metres down. It's a machine with a big spinning drum on the front that cuts the potash straight out of the seam, no blasting, and a conveyor carries it back to the shuttle cars. I lead a panel crew of six, and I've got two apprentices this year, Jono and Priya, who I'm teaching to read the seam. The best feeling is a long clean cut where the drum sings and the floor stays flat. What wears me out is the cage ride at the end of the day, fifteen minutes in a steel box with everyone too tired to talk.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married Amina last year, she works at the pharmacy in Felton. We'd like children in a couple of years, God willing. The wedding cleaned us out, and I send money to my mother since my father passed, so we've got maybe two weeks saved. Felton pays less than the big potash mines further west, but it's the only mine here, so you take what's offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Most new things at work end up as one more screen you ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's get back to training young people properly. Everyone wanted to talk about AI, and meanwhile we can't find enough apprentices. I'd say it at the mosque, too, the older men like to hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. I use the AI now and then, mostly to translate the German manuals for the cutter head, and it's handy, but I don't need it to be more than that. It means my plan stays my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the crew and keep taking apprentices. I'd try to get savings up to two months before we try for a baby, maybe by picking up Sunday maintenance shifts. And I'd ask for the trainer allowance, because I'm doing the training without it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Steady, like a good cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the manuals. How does that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cutter head comes from a company in Germany, and the manual's in German with bad English beside it. I take a photo and ask the AI what it says. It's right most of the time, and when it isn't, I ring the supplier's man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your plan look like, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two months saved, then a baby, then a small house in maybe five years. Keep running the panel till I'm 40, then go up to the surface as a supervisor. It's not fancy, but it's how my father did it, more or less.

S0.say: Good, let's get back to training young people properly; everyone talked about AI while we can't find enough apprentices. I'd say it at the mosque too.
S0.think: I'd be glad. I use AI now and then to translate German manuals, and it's handy, but I don't need more than that. My plan stays my plan.
S0.do: Keeps leading his crew and training apprentices, picks up Sunday maintenance shifts to build two months of savings before trying for a baby, and asks for a trainer allowance.
S0.feel: Calm and steady, like a good cut.
S0.quote: It's not fancy, but it's how my father did it, more or less.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro has a clear, traditional life plan tied to his father's example. He uses AI in a practical, limited way and checks with a real person when it fails. Training apprentices is a big part of who he is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I can believe. They're already testing a remote-control miner at the big potash mine out west.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company should bring people along, with proper training on the new machines, the way they trained my father on the first continuous miners. Change is fine if it's done with respect. I'd say the apprentices should learn both the old way and the new way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be watching closely. The miner is a big, simple, repeated job, cut, back up, cut, so it makes sense to automate. I'd be fine if I move early enough, but I'd want to see it working first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the remote miner had run a year at the western mine without stopping every hour, I'd ask to train on it. I'd keep my apprentices close and make sure Jono and Priya get the training too. And we'd hold off the baby a little until I knew where I stood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not afraid, but alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off the baby. How does Amina feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say it's my worry, not hers. She'd say we'll manage, her mother had five kids on a miner's pay. And she's probably right, but I'd still want to know the job is there first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for a full year at the other mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen new equipment arrive with a big ceremony and leave quietly six months later. A year shows you the bad months, the floods, the breakdowns. If it lasts a year, it's real.

S1.say: The company should bring people along with proper training, the way they trained my father on the first continuous miners. Change is fine if done with respect, and apprentices should learn both ways.
S1.think: The miner is a simple repeated job, so it makes sense to automate. I'd be fine if I move early enough, but I'd want to see it working first.
S1.do: Asks to train on the remote miner once it has run a full year at another mine, and makes sure his apprentices get trained too. Holds off on starting a family until he knows where he stands.
S1.quote: A year shows you the bad months, the floods, the breakdowns. If it lasts a year, it's real.
S1.fieldNote: Pedro's test for new technology is simple: does it survive a full year of real conditions. He thinks of his apprentices as much as himself. His caution about having a child contrasts with his wife's calmer view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's too fast. That's before my apprentices even finish their time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong to let this happen so fast that families can't adjust. I'm a free market man, but a market needs people with wages to buy things. I'd say families and communities would have to hold each other up, because the government won't be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be very worried. Two weeks of savings, a mother to support, a wife who wants children. If a robot can run the miner and fix it too, then what's left down there for me?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, Amina and I would sit down and put off children for now, which would be hard. I'd keep sending my mother money but less, and ask my brother Yusuf, who runs a tyre shop in Felton, if there's work for me there on weekends straight away. I'd save every cent of overtime while the mine still runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the cage stopping halfway up and the lights going off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two years change, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I don't have time to train for anything and finish. My apprentices don't finish either, which hurts more, because I promised them a trade. In a longer one, I could at least see them through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Yusuf's tyre shop. Wouldn't robots reach that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, in time. But a family shop in a small town is the last place to buy a robot, they can't afford one. And at least with family, you look after each other while you work out the next thing.

S2.say: It's wrong to let this move so fast families can't adjust. I believe in the free market, but a market needs people with wages, and communities would have to hold each other up.
S2.think: I'd be very worried, with two weeks of savings, a mother to support and a wife who wants children. If a robot runs and fixes the miner, what's left for me?
S2.do: Agrees with his wife to postpone having children, reduces money sent to his mother, and asks his brother for weekend work at the family tyre shop straight away. Saves every bit of overtime while the mine still runs.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the cage stopping halfway up with the lights off.
S2.quote: My apprentices don't finish either, which hurts more, because I promised them a trade.
S2.fieldNote: His sharpest pain is broken promises to his apprentices, more than his own job. He balances free-market views with a belief that wages keep markets alive. He turns to family business rather than government for a lifeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's tight, but my apprentices could finish and I could make a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to turn every mine into a training ground for whatever comes next. Apprenticeships, not just payouts. I'd say it to the managers, at the mosque, and to the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd guess I have three years on the miner before they bring in the remote ones, and maybe two after that running them. That's enough to save a little and learn something. I don't know what's safe, but I'd take my chances with a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for the mine's maintenance planning course, because someone has to schedule all those machines. I'd get Jono and Priya through their tickets. We'd try for a baby around year two, once I had the new role, and keep saving overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd be moving, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years give you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They let me keep my word to the apprentices, and that matters to me. And they let us have a child without it being a gamble. Two years is a fall, five years is a climb down with a rope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Did anything change in your thinking about who should help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Family first, then the community, then the company. The government can help by paying for apprenticeships, but I don't want a cheque in the mail for doing nothing.

S3.say: We have five years to turn every mine into a training ground for what comes next: apprenticeships, not just payouts. I'd say it to managers, at the mosque and to the council.
S3.think: I've maybe got three years on the miner and two running the remote ones, enough to save a little and learn something. I don't know what's safe, but I'd bet on a trade.
S3.do: Signs up for the mine's maintenance planning course in year one and sees both apprentices through their qualifications. Plans to try for a baby around year two once in the new role, while saving overtime.
S3.quote: Two years is a fall, five years is a climb down with a rope.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets Pedro keep his promise to his apprentices and plan a child, which eases him a lot. His order of help stays fixed: family, community, company, then government paying for apprenticeships. He rejects money for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a good long run to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it right, so the companies and families have no excuse. Train the young ones in the new machines, keep the older ones on as long as they're useful. I'd say it plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be fine. A child, the remote miner, then maintenance planning, and maybe something with Yusuf on the side. The worry is only that in ten years everything ends at the same place, so I'd need a plan for after, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the panel for a few years and train on the remote miner once it's proven, maybe year three. Amina and I would try for a baby next year. I'd also put in two Saturdays a month at Yusuf's shop and save that money separately, as our little emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. It's like knowing winter is coming in ten years. You cut wood every summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd need a plan for after. What might that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe there's no job left for anybody, and then we're all in the same boat, which is strange comfort. Until then, I'd keep my family close and my hands busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jono and Priya in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish your ticket, then learn the remote system, then learn to fix it. Three things in ten years. And keep your money in two places, one for living and one for the bad day.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do it right, so companies and families have no excuse. Train the young ones on the new machines and keep the older ones on while they're useful.
S4.think: We'd be fine: a child, the remote miner, then maintenance planning, maybe something with Yusuf on the side. But everything ends at the same place, so I'd need a plan for after too.
S4.do: Keeps running his panel, trains on the remote miner around year three once proven, and plans to try for a baby next year. Works two Saturdays a month at his brother's tyre shop and saves that money as an emergency fund.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, like cutting wood every summer for a winter ten years off.
S4.quote: It's like knowing winter is coming in ten years. You cut wood every summer.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Pedro builds his life plan around the change rather than putting it off. He's honest that the end point is the same in all three AGI pictures and he has no answer for after. His advice to apprentices shows his steady, step-by-step way of thinking.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is the companies paying to finish every apprenticeship they started, and help for small family businesses to take on workers from the mines. Something that keeps people working, not just paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what work means to a man like me. It's not only money. When I come up in the cage, dirty and tired, I know I earned my dinner. I'd want my son to have that feeling, however it comes.

headlineQuote: When I come up in the cage, dirty and tired, I know I earned my dinner.
portrait: Pedro Usman is a 27-year-old continuous-miner operator and panel crew lead at an underground potash mine, newly married to Amina and supporting his widowed mother on two weeks of savings. He trains two apprentices and uses AI now and then to translate equipment manuals. He's calm in the plateau and uneasy in steady disruption, waiting a year to see remote miners proven before he trains. Two-year AGI alarms him, mostly because his apprentices wouldn't finish, and makes him delay children and lean on his brother's tyre shop. With five and ten years he plans training, a child and a small emergency fund, always putting family and work before handouts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to retrain, see his apprentices through or start a family.
whatWouldHelp: Companies paying to finish every apprenticeship they started, and help for small family businesses to take on workers from the mines.
